To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the distribution of error rates is important, 2) the Gini Coefficients is an effective metric for capturing this distribution, 3) the selection of the features, the classifier, and the attacker model all significantly influence the error distribution, 4) researchers should be careful when selecting features to optimize the EER, 5) the selection of training samples and imposter data significantly influence the EER and should be clearly reported.

1) the mean error rate does not accurately capture the distribution of errors and can therefore be misleading; 2) some biometric features are particularly susceptible to systematic errors and should be avoided when designing systems; 3) some feature selection and classifier optimization techniques can lead to lower error rates but also increase the prevalence of systematic attacks; 4) the inclusion of imposter data or the random selection of training data can lead to significant under- estimation of error rates and can therefore be considered as

(i) the inclusion of some features can increase the prevalence of systematic false accept errors, which is a serious security issue, (ii) the Gini coefficient is a good metric to measure this phenomenon, and (iii) the selection of training and testing datasets is crucial to obtain accurate error rates.
